prose_changes.old: The same monastic tradition continues directly as Athonite monasticism and, through it, the wider Orthodox monastic world. Its theology of the image became settled Orthodox doctrine. It is the reason icons look the way they do and are treated the way they are in Orthodox churches today, and the Sunday of Orthodoxy, kept every year on the first Sunday of Lent, is a liturgical commemoration of how this argument ended. Theodore's reorganization of Stoudios also shaped later Byzantine and Slavic monastic rules well beyond his own house.
prose_changes.new: The monks' way of life carried on after 843, and Stoudios still had its monks two centuries later. Athonite monks are usually counted their heirs, and through them the wider Orthodox monastic world, though little survives to show the handover. The monks' theology of the image became settled Orthodox teaching. It is why icons look the way they do in Orthodox churches today, and why people treat them as they do. The Sunday of Orthodoxy, kept each year on the first Sunday of Lent, still marks how the argument ended. Theodore's rule for Stoudios also shaped later Byzantine and Slavic rules for monks, well beyond his own house.
prose_changes.reason: 'Continues directly as Athonite monasticism' stated as fact a line the vendored texts show only thinly (Inferential-Thin: Sabbas of Stoudios at Nicaea II in 787; Niketas Stethatos of Stoudios c. 1030). The rewrite says what is shown and states the gap plainly. The paragraph scored FRE 36 / FK 13.6, so it is rewritten whole; the other claims are kept (image theology, Sunday of Orthodoxy, Theodore's rule, now carried by the Photius and Kyiv Caves links). 'Reorganization' becomes 'rule', the word Mouravieff uses.

prose_changes.old: The Bogomils take their name from a Bulgarian priest of the mid-tenth century, and the earliest account of them — a long sermon written against them by another priest, Cosmas. Describes a movement of ascetics who rejected almost everything the visible church consisted of: church buildings, the cross, icons, the sacraments, infant baptism and the clergy who administered them. Behind that refusal, the sources report, lay a conviction that the material world and the human body were not made by God at all but by a fallen power, so that the whole apparatus of physical religion was a mistake. They spread from Bulgaria through the Balkans and into Byzantium, where around 1100 their most prominent teacher, a man called Basil, was burned in Constantinople. As with the Paulicians, none of their own writing survives: everything described here is the report of people arguing against them.
prose_changes.new: The Bogomils take their name from a Bulgarian priest of the mid-tenth century. The earliest account of them is a long sermon written against them by another priest, Cosmas. It describes ascetics who rejected almost all that the visible church was made of: church buildings, the cross, icons, the sacraments, infant baptism and the clergy who gave them. Behind that refusal, the sources say, lay a belief that God did not make the material world or the human body. A fallen power made them, so the whole machinery of bodily religion was a mistake. The movement spread from Bulgaria through the Balkans and into Byzantium. There, around 1100, its best-known teacher, a man called Basil, was burned in Constantinople. As with the Paulicians, none of their own writing survives. All we know of them comes from the people who argued against them.
prose_changes.reason: The sentence naming Cosmas's sermon was broken: 'and the earliest account of them — a long sermon written against them by another priest, Cosmas. Describes a movement ...' No claim added or removed; Cosmas's sermon is cited by Rački (pp. 94-95) and Evans (pp. xxxv-xxxvi), and the census lists it among the hostile sources.

escalations: Census structure (overlap): bogomils is dated '10th c. onward' and balkan-bogomil-continuation covers 1054-1300. Basil's burning (c. 1100) and the Cathar claim (Sacconi, 1250) fall in both windows and are named in both texts. I drafted the Cathar link from bogomils, because its text names it three times, and treated Basil as out of scope here (the era-5 entry owns it). Decision wanted: should bogomils end at 1054 and the Cathar link move to the continuation, or stay here?

Census structure (boundary): the macedonian entry (843-1054) says it 'receives the 1054 schism itself', while the existing Documented break and argued-against links for 1054 sit on byzantine-church-after-1054, whose summary puts Cerularius on its side. I did not duplicate them. If Mark wants the macedonian entry to carry 1054 too, the same Mirbt sources would serve.

Rule question (repeats the era-2 escalation): several standard facts in my movements have no vendored source (Stephen the Younger's death in 765; Theodore's beatings and exiles; Tephrike's fall in 878; the Paulician alliance with the Arabs; the 1965 revocation; the Photian schism and the Filioque writings). I left them standing and listed the texts in wants rather than rewriting them as 'may have'.

Grade method check: five new links rest on secondary works only (Rački 1869, Evans 1877, Mouravieff 1842, Lutzow 1910) and are graded Dominant Modern Reconstruction, the highest grade a secondary-only link can take. These are nineteenth- and early twentieth-century works, not modern reconstructions. If 'Dominant Modern Reconstruction' should be kept for current scholarship, these drop to Inferential-Thin; that would be a method ruling.
